source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli, De Angeli (2026) Are Semantic Networks Associated with Idea Originality in Artificial Creativity? A Comparison with Human Agents
finding: Direct test of the Mednick/Kenett idea on an LLM. ChatGPT-4o was run as 81 simulated participants on verbal fluency, free association and the Alternate Uses Task. Semantic networks were built from fluency and association output and compared with 81 students split by AUT originality.
numbers: Fluency: GPT 43.8 (SD 5.36), high-creative humans 19.1, low-creative 12.2; F(2,159)=438, p<.001, partial eta2=.846.
limits: One model, chat interface, hyperparameters unknown, one prompt, no time limit for the model, psychology students only, preprint.
agent_relevance: Our agent produces far more items than people. Fluency alone is not a sign of a flexible network.

source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli, De Angeli (2026) Are Semantic Networks Associated with Idea Originality in Artificial Creativity? A Comparison with Human Agents
finding: Originality order was high-creative humans > GPT-4o > low-creative humans. GPT-4o is more original than weak human thinkers but below strong ones.
numbers: AUT originality, total production: GPT>LCH B=0.03 SE=.013 p=.048; GPT<HCH B=-0.12 p<.001; HCH>LCH B=0.15 p<.001. Top-3 peaks: GPT 2.25, LCH 2.00, HCH 2.59. Two blind coders ICC=.93.
limits: AUT may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Model originality sits mid-range and is narrow (low variance). Distance control must aim at the high tail, not the mean.

source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli, De Angeli (2026) Are Semantic Networks Associated with Idea Originality in Artificial Creativity? A Comparison with Human Agents
finding: GPT-4o semantic network had longer paths than both human groups, the reverse of Mednick's prediction if originality came from short paths. Network flexibility order was HCH > LCH > GPT, but originality put GPT above LCH. The network-originality link did not carry over to the machine.
numbers: Average shortest path length: GPT 4.378, LCH 3.429, HCH 3.325; F(2,2996)=2430.56, partial eta2=.619. GPT vs LCH d=2.32, GPT vs HCH d=2.55. HCH vs LCH d=0.42.
limits: Networks built from short fluency and association tasks with edges as covariate; path length may partly reflect output volume and vocabulary choice.
agent_relevance: Human network metrics cannot be read directly onto an LLM. Do not use path length of model output as a creativity proxy for the agent.

source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli, De Angeli (2026) Are Semantic Networks Associated with Idea Originality in Artificial Creativity? A Comparison with Human Agents
finding: Clustering was almost equal across groups, modularity was higher for GPT, and percolation (resilience to node removal) was lowest for GPT, so its network was more fragile. The human high-vs-low gap was small.
numbers: Clustering: GPT .705, LCH .710, HCH .715 (eta2=.19). Modularity Q: GPT .692, LCH .666, HCH .662 (eta2=.386). Percolation integral: GPT 77.9, LCH 85.2, HCH 85.8; GPT vs LCH d=4.01; HCH vs LCH d=0.32, t(949)=5.04. Human ASPL/CC/Q d = 0.42/0.41/0.20.
limits: Single human sample of 81.
agent_relevance: Replication note: in this sample the human high-creative network was only slightly more flexible, consistent with a small effect as in Kenett 2014.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the Creativity of Large Language Models: Can models produce divergent semantic association?
finding: Uses the Divergent Association Task (mean cosine distance of GloVe vectors over words the model lists as unrelated). GPT-4 with greedy decoding beats most people. This measures how far apart a model can place its seed concepts.
numbers: GPT-4 greedy DAT 89.1, above 96.1% of humans. GPT-3.5-turbo 80.8, above average human. Smaller open models below the human mean, roughly in line with size.
limits: DAT uses word embeddings; word frequency is a confound. Models are 2023 snapshots (gpt-4-0314).
agent_relevance: Instructed distance is cheap: telling the model to produce unrelated words moves it far out. This is the basis for O7 seed distance control.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the Creativity of Large Language Models: Can models produce divergent semantic association?
finding: Temperature and top-p sampling raise DAT for every model except GPT-4, but also make output unstable and invalid. For GPT-4 the highest-probability tokens already match high-quality divergent answers.
numbers: Temperature varied 0.1 to 1; top-p 0.9 with t=0.7 as the stochastic default. Effect positive but limited for non-GPT-4 models.
limits: Temperature only up to 1. Small models only for the positive effect.
agent_relevance: Random sampling is a weak distance knob. Prefer explicit instruction over heat for a strong model.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the Creativity of Large Language Models: Can models produce divergent semantic association?
finding: Control conditions show the instruction does the work. With a plain 'write 10 nouns' prompt, models give related words; with the DAT or 'random' prompt they spread out. A naive WordNet random noun sampler also beats most humans and models.
numbers: Three prompt conditions: Base, Random, DAT. After controlling for surprisal, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo still beat average human, but GPT-4's lead shrinks.
limits: The WordNet baseline shows DAT can be gamed by rare words. Distance without coherence is not creativity.
agent_relevance: Pair any distance target with a relevance or usefulness check, because random distance scores high.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024, v2 2025) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark of many LLMs against a human DAT sample of about 100,000 people. GPT-4 is above the human mean and Gemini Pro is indistinguishable from it. The top human decile, quartile and above-median groups still beat every model tested.
numbers: Human sample 100,000. LLM means from 500 responses each. GPT-4-turbo scored lower than GPT-4, so newer releases are not always better.
limits: Authors say LLMs may reach scores by different processes. GloVe distance is one facet only.
agent_relevance: Model upper tail is below human upper tail. Do not assume a scaffold can reach top-human distance by prompting alone.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024, v2 2025) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Models repeat the same far words. GPT-4 put 'microscope' in 70% of sets and 'elephant' in 60%; GPT-4-turbo put 'ocean' in over 90%. Humans' most common word was 'car' at 1.4%.
numbers: Word repetition rates as stated. Every model beat a no-divergence control (p<.001).
limits: A high-DAT list can hide a collapsed vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Seed words for O7 need an anti-repeat memory across calls, since high distance can come from a stuck favorite list.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024, v2 2025) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Prompt strategy and temperature both change DAT. Naming a strategy such as 'varying etymology' beat the plain DAT prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; thesaurus also beat it for GPT-4; meaning opposition was worse. Higher temperature raised GPT-4 scores.
numbers: GPT-4 at the highest temperature (1.5) had mean 85.6, above 72% of humans (below the 89.1 greedy figure in Chen and Ding, so scoring set-ups differ). Strategy contrasts all significant except thesaurus vs basic.
limits: Absolute DAT numbers differ between pipelines; compare within one paper only.
agent_relevance: Concrete lexical-strategy instruction (etymology, other domains) is a usable seed-distance prompt. Opposition is not.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2024, v2 2025) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: Distance transfer to longer text is weaker. In haiku, synopsis and flash-fiction tasks a semantic integration score rose with temperature for synopses and flash fiction but not for haikus, which stayed on the nature theme.
numbers: Haiku cosine to 'nature' stayed high at temperatures 0.6 to 1.4; DSI effect of temperature non-significant for haiku.
limits: Embedding-based DSI only.
agent_relevance: Seed distance set at word level does not guarantee a distant final product. Check the output, not only the seeds.

source: Patel, Crossman, Aggarwal, Wenger (2026) Are LLMs becoming similarly creative? Evidence from three years of models
finding: Across 68 models released March 2023 to July 2026, cross-family embedding distance of Alternate Uses answers fell. Newer models converge on the same uses.
numbers: AUT mean cross-family cosine distance from about 0.50 to below 0.40. Slope -0.01385 per release bin, 95% CI [-0.01695, -0.01044]. Infinity-Chat slope -0.00167 [-0.00267, -0.00074]. All 1,000 bootstrap runs negative.
limits: Preliminary; sentence embeddings; sampled models vary by bin; trend not shown to persist.
agent_relevance: Shared associations across models are growing. Several different models as seed sources give less spread than before.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Study of 70+ models on 26K open-ended real queries. Models repeat themselves (intra-model) and each other (inter-model). Diversity-oriented decoding does not fix it.
numbers: Same-prompt average pairwise similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases. Inter-model similarity 0.71 to 0.82 (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; vs gpt-4o 0.81). Under min-p, 81% of pairs exceed 0.7 and 61.2% exceed 0.8. 25 annotators per item, 31,250 annotations.
limits: Sentence-embedding similarity; main run top-p 0.9, t=1.0.
agent_relevance: Associative paths are shared across models. A multi-model ensemble is not a source of independent seeds.

source: Schapiro, Park, Sosa, Varshney (2026) CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
finding: A weight-steering method raises DAT without behavior data. It worked on six small open models (3B to 14B: Llama, Qwen, Phi) and beat prompting, sampling parameters and activation steering.
numbers: DAT gain up to 14 human percentile points. Average percentile with CN 94.1 vs activation steering 93.9; prompt-only steering 87.8 vs prompting 87.9.
limits: Needs weight access, so not usable on a hosted model behind an API. Percentiles use the human distribution of Wang et al. 2025.
agent_relevance: Out of reach for a scaffold-only agent. Shows the baseline can be shifted; our lever is the prompt.

source: Schapiro, Park, Sosa, Varshney (2026) CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse
finding: Mode collapse is large even on DAT. Baseline models put 25.5% of tokens on their own top-10 words. Galaxy, quasar and xylophone sit in the top 30 of every model family. CN cut top-10 share by 10.2 points and raised vocabulary entropy by 0.59 nats (+10%).
numbers: Human evaluation N=720 on AUT and a second task. Originality gain average d=+0.40. Activation steering matched CN on DAT but did not transfer to AUT.
limits: Rater sample and moderate effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Explicit used-word lists in the prompt might cut this collapse cheaply. Untested here.

source: Moon, Johnson, et al. (2026) Thinking Outside the Bots: Human Ideas in AI's Semantic Blind Spots Are Not Inferior
finding: EDGE method maps how far each human idea lies from a matched pool of GPT-5-mini ideas in embedding space. Human ideas far from the AI pool were not worse. For humans, more distinctive ideas got higher creativity ratings; for AI ideas the link was weak or reversed.
numbers: Tasks: admissions essays, AUT (241 people, brick and knife, 481 bundles), interpersonal advice. Three embedding models. 481 GPT-5-mini AUT bundles matched to human bundles.
limits: Not peer reviewed. Some creativity scores come from fine-tuned model raters.
agent_relevance: Supports distance from the model's own default as a useful target. But for the model, distance did not predict rated creativity, so check quality separately.

source: Zhang and Ma (2026) Psychometric Comparability of LLM-Based Digital Twins (word association study)
finding: Compares human Small World of Words networks with LLM World of Words networks (Mistral-7b, Llama3.1-8b, Claude-3.5-haiku) on 86 Big Five keywords and two other word lists. All networks are small-world, but LLM networks share few nodes, have lower centrality and only partial community overlap.
numbers: Fewer than half of nodes shared. Humans had higher degree centrality than every LLM network on all three lists. Claude-3.5-haiku had much higher small-worldness (higher normalized clustering, longer normalized path). Community agreement above random but modest.
limits: Cue-based free association only; no creativity score.
agent_relevance: Small-world shape, found in humans by Kenett, also appears in LLM association, so small-worldness alone does not separate creative from non-creative.

source: Abramski, Improta, Rossetti, Stella (2024) The LLM World of Words English free association norms generated by large language models
finding: Dataset of LLM free associations for about 12,000 SWOW cues from Mistral, Llama3 and Haiku, used to build semantic memory networks comparable to human ones. Gives a way to read network structure from a model by prompting.
numbers: Full networks: Humans 116,640 nodes, 1,164,026 edges, mean degree 20.0; Mistral 42,073 / 417,697 / 19.9; Llama3 105,777 / 770,458 / 14.6; Haiku 17,679 / 77,698 / 8.8. Edge overlap with humans 13% to 23%.
limits: Haiku network is much sparser. Gender-stereotype demo, no creativity measure.
agent_relevance: A usable probe: ask the model for associates of a seed, build the graph, measure path length between candidate seed pairs before choosing O7 seeds.

source: Abramski, Improta, Rossetti, Stella (2024) The LLM World of Words English free association norms generated by large language models
finding: Reduced networks show how much models differ from humans in structure, and the paper runs spreading activation (spreadr) on both.
numbers: Reduced (WordNet, edges weight>1, largest component): Humans 24,308 nodes, 317,344 edges, density .0011; Mistral 20,339 / 199,103; Llama3 38,987 / 546,866; Haiku 15,596 / 64,599. Common nodes 59% Mistral, 48% Llama3, 57% Haiku.
limits: Only R1 to R3 responses.
agent_relevance: Model choice changes the associative graph a lot. A Haiku-class model gives a narrow graph.

source: Heineman, Koenen, Varma (2024) Towards a path dependent account of category fluency
finding: Tests two accounts of memory search: optimal foraging (Hills 2012) and random walk on a semantic network (Abbott 2015). Both give identical patch-switch results. The paper turns them into sequence generators and adds an LLM that predicts the next animal from the full prior list. Even the LLM needs a global switch cue.
numbers: Compared generated lists to human lists by n-gram overlap. A category bias and an LLM non-Markov account fit human data better. Deterministic search on the network was needed to reproduce human behavior.
limits: Category fluency (animals), not creativity. Overlap metric.
agent_relevance: Closest computational model of search over a semantic network rebuilt with an LLM. Agents need an explicit switch cue to leave a topic patch.

source: Ismayilzada, Luchini, ..., Beaty (2026) Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking
finding: fMRI from 170 people doing the Alternate Uses Task compared with LLM representations (270M to 72B parameters) by RSA in default mode and frontoparietal networks. Alignment rises with idea originality and, in the default network, with model size. A creativity-tuned Llama-3.1-8B kept alignment with high-creativity responses; a reasoning-trained variant showed negative alignment to them.
numbers: N=170. Alignment clearest early in the creative process.
limits: Representation alignment, not path-length measures. Only the abstract and first page were read closely.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-style post-training may move a model away from the neural geometry of creative thought. Keep reasoning mode and open mode apart.

source: Moon, Cho, Borrajo, Ganesh, Hashemi (2026) Breaking Homogeneity: Diversifying Persona Sets for Creative LLM Outputs
finding: Persona-set conditioning widens outputs. Evolutionary persona generation raised AUT response diversity 78.8%, originality 26.1%, flexibility 49.5%, holistic creativity 13.9% over task-only prompting, validity 98.5%. On DAT the gain is tiny.
numbers: DAT: task only 89.13, evolution 89.48, creative prompt 86.05, DMAD 90.62, DMAD plus evolution 90.93. Infinity-Chat homogeneity 0.946 to 0.798. Generator Gemma-4-31B, judge Qwen3.6-27B.
limits: DAT near ceiling. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Different personas act as different seed anchors. A cheap scaffold route to shift associative start points.

source: Kenett, Anaki, Faust (2014) Investigating the structure of semantic networks in low and high creative persons
finding: Founding network study named in the subfield brief: networks of high-creative people had shorter paths and more spread-out links than low-creative people. Not opened this session; the human-side angles should read it. Domanti et al. (2026) build their hypotheses on it.
numbers: Per subfield brief: small effect, 139 people across key works. Not verified here.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Defines the human effect the LLM studies above try to map.

source: Olson, Nahas, Chmoulevitch, Cropper, Webb (2021) Naming unrelated words predicts creativity
finding: Source of the Divergent Association Task and its human norms, used by all DAT-on-LLM papers above (Chen and Ding cite it for the 7-word rule). Not opened.
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Anchors the distance measure the agent could compute.

source: Hubert, Awa, Zabelina (2024) The current state of artificial intelligence generative language models is more creative than humans on divergent thinking tasks
finding: Cited by Domanti et al. (2026) among studies where machines scored better than people on creativity tests. Not opened.
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Second-hand via Domanti.
agent_relevance: One of the 'GenAI better' results in a mixed literature.

source: Mixed LLM vs human findings listed by Domanti et al. (2026): Cropley 2023, Hubert 2024, Guzik 2023, Haase and Hanel 2023, Stevenson 2022, Bangerl 2024
finding: Domanti et al. sum up the field as contradictory: some studies show machines ahead (Cropley 2023, Hubert 2024, Guzik 2023), one equal (Haase and Hanel 2023), others humans ahead (Stevenson 2022, Bangerl 2024). They say most share a product-centred definition and cannot explain process.
numbers: Citation list only; primary papers not opened.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one 'LLMs beat humans' headline. Process-level checks matter.
